description_full: IDACORP, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the generation, transmission, distribution, purchase, and sale of electric energy in the United States. The company operates 17 hydropower generating plants located in southern Idaho and eastern Oregon; and three natural gas-fired plants situated in southern Idaho, as well as interests in a coal-fired and natural gas-fired steam generating plant located in Wyoming; and interests in a coal-fired steam generating plant situated in Nevada. As of December 31, 2025, it had approximately 4,730 pole miles of high-voltage transmission lines; 23 step-up transmission substations located at power plants; 21 transmission substations; 12 switching stations; 31 mixed-use transmission and distribution substations; 188 energized distribution substations; approximately 30,020 linear miles of distribution lines; and a capacity of 1,228 MWh of battery storage. The company provides electric utility services to approximately 664,000 retail customers in southern Idaho and eastern Oregon. It serves commercial and industrial customers, which involved in food processing, electronics and general manufacturing, agriculture, health care, government, education, and information technology. The company also invests in housing and other real estate tax credit investments. IDACORP, Inc. was founded in 1915 and is headquartered in Boise, Idaho.

financial_summary: IDACORP, Inc. is a mid-cap utilities business with a $8.6B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $577M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.3× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
